_howTo: Radio talks with Walla Walla, typed out on the slip. Each lesson has two: "start" comes on as the lesson opens, and "check" is a short quiz once the lesson's check is done. Each talk has turns; in each turn Walla Walla says "them" and the player picks one of up to three "replies" (none means a plain "Roger. Over."). A reply can have a "back" line, and "right": true marks the right answer to a question (it is never scored). Every reply leads on to the next turn.

turns.them: W7HAR, this is W7DQ, Walla Walla. Fifteen years, and the same old crackle. Are you still up there, Harrow?

replies.back: Older is the only direction anybody goes.
They took our sets off the air for the war. Now we’re back on, and so am I.

turns.them: Have you seen the papers? A fellow at General Electric, Schaefer, dropped dry ice on a cloud over Massachusetts ten days ago and made it snow. On purpose. There’s a new workbook on the train: how it works, and how much of it to believe.

replies.back: That’s the lesson. Read it, and I’ll have questions at the end.

replies.say: Sounds like the rainmakers at the county fair.
replies.back: That’s what I said. Then I read the report. This one is real physics. Mostly.

turns.them: Harrow, Walla Walla. Last questions in the book. A cloud at −3 °C. Which will make it snow?

replies.back: By sheer cold. Silver iodide doesn’t wake up until about −5.
Not yet at −3. It wants about −5 or colder. Dry ice works at any temperature below freezing.
Dry ice does. It makes its own ice by sheer cold.

turns.them: Somebody seeds a layer with far too many crystals. What happens?

replies.say: They stay too small to fall.
replies.back: Right. Overseeding: the water is shared out too thin.
More crystals share the same water, so each stays small and none of them fall. That’s overseeding.
Hail needs a thunderstorm’s updraught. Too many crystals just stay too small to fall.

turns.them: A man says he seeded five storms last winter and got forty percent more snow. What does that prove?

replies.say: Nothing. He picked the storms himself.
replies.back: Right. Storms picked by chance, a control area, and many winters, or nothing.
Five storms he picked himself is a good eye for weather, not proof. A fair trial picks by chance, over many winters.
It does, sometimes, a little. That’s the trouble: a little is hard to see past luck.

turns.them: A fellow who is honest about small numbers is worth ten who promise big ones. That’s the last of it, Harrow. Seventy-three.
